The Clique Structure of Johnson Graphs

Pavel Shuldiner & R. Wayne Oldford Affiliation: University of Waterloo
Abstract

Motivated by an approach to visualization of high dimensional statistical data given in Hurley & Oldford ((2011)), this work examines the clique structure of Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) Johnson graphs. Cliques and maximal cliques are characterized and proved to be of one of only two types. These types are characterized by features of the intersection and of the union of the subsets of [n]={1,2,…,n}[n]=\{1,2,\ldots,n\} which define the vertices of the graph. Clique numbers and clique partition numbers follow. The results on Johnson graphs are connected to results on intersecting families of sets related to extremal set theory.

Keywords: Clique covers, clique enumeration, graph enumeration, intersecting families, quotient graph.

AMS classification: 05C30 (Primary), 05D05 (Secondary)

1 Introduction

Let [n][n] denote the set of the first nn positive integers {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\ldots,n\} and ([n]m)\binom{[n]}{m} the collection of all subsets of [n][n] of size mm. The Johnson graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), denoted Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1), has (nm)\binom{n}{m} vertices/nodes v∈Vv\in V, each labelled by a unique set ν⁡(v)∈([n]m)\nu(v)\in\binom{[n]}{m}, and (nm)​m⁡(n−m)2\binom{n}{m}\frac{m(n-m)}{2} undirected edges ei​j∈Ee_{ij}\in E between distinct nodes viv_{i} and vjv_{j} if, and only if, |ν⁡(vi)∩ν⁡(vj)|=m−1|{\nu(v_{i})\cap\nu(v_{j})}|=m-1. Figure 1 shows two examples – J4​(2,1)J_{4}(2,1) in (a) and J5​(3,2)J_{5}(3,2) in (b).

Our motivation for studying Johnson graphs originates with the problem of visual exploration of high dimensional data. If there are NN observations on nn variables in a statistical data set, then the data can be thought of as a set of NN points in nn dimensional real space. Such data are most naturally viewed in 22 and 33 dimensional scatterplots. Hurley & Oldford ((2011)) suggest interpreting a Jn​(2,1)J_{n}(2,1) Johnson graph as having 22-dimensional spaces as its nodes (defined by the indices of the variables) and, as its edges, 33-dimensional spaces defined by the union of the variables defining the adjacent nodes (e.g., see Figure 1(a) for n=4n=4). The Johnson graph provides a “navigation graph” for exploring high dimensional point clouds along lower dimensional trajectories. Following a path along the graph traverses from one 2​d2d-space to another along 3​d3d-transitions. Dynamic 3​d3d-scatterplot rotations from one 2​d2d-space to another have been used effectively in data analysis (Oldford & Waddell, (2011); Waddell & Oldford, (2022), e.g., see), as has static displays of large numbers of 2​d2d-scatterplots laid out by following paths in the Jn​(2,1)J_{n}(2,1) with neighbouring scatterplots sharing a common axis (Hofert & Oldford, (2017); Hofert & Oldford, (2020), e.g., see). Hurley & Oldford ((2011)) also consider using paths along Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) Johnson graphs in conjunction with more complex visualizations to perceive structure in point clouds of dimension m≥3m\geq 3. Understanding the clique structure of the Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) for arbitrary mm will help data analysts better understand, and make use of, lower dimensional regions of the full nn-dimensional space of the data.

In what follows, focus is on characterizing the structure of cliques, particularly maximal cliques in the Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) Johnson graph. Section 2 begins with some preliminary results for the Jn​(2,1)J_{n}(2,1) Johnson graph of interest in our motivating example. This section illustrates the logic, and provides the base case, for many of the more general results developed in Section 3 for the Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) Johnson graph. Results in both sections are derived without reference to the motivating example. These include the characterization of maximal cliques (there are only two types) of a Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1), from which follows the clique number. Section 4 characterizes the nature of any rr-clique, from which the clique partition number follows in Section 4.1.

Johnson “graphs are important because they enable us to translate many combinatorial problems about sets into graph theory” (Godsil & Royle, (2001), p. 9). Section 5 discusses the results of earlier sections in the context of the intersecting families of sets from extremal set theory Gerbner & Patkós ((2018)). Shuldiner & Oldford ((2022)) showed how intersecting families of sets can also be related to cliques in a clique cover. The last section ends with some discussion on the implications of the results in the context of the motivating example of statistical data analysis.

The intersection

  • •

    of H1H_{1} is S1=∩v∈H1ν(v)={1}S_{1}=\cap_{v\in H_{1}}~\nu(v)=\{1\},

Of special interest is the relationship between this intersection set and cliques, HH of GG (e.g., H1H_{1} and H2H_{2} above; not H3H_{3}). For example, for a clique HH to be maximal (i.e., no larger clique contains HH) in a Jn​(2,1)J_{n}(2,1) graph, it is easy to see that the size of its intersection set is either 1 (e.g., |S1|=1|{S_{1}}|=1) or 0 (e.g., |S2|=0|{S_{2}}|=0), as shown below in Lemma 2.1.

Lemma 2.1.

For G=Jn​(2,1)G=J_{n}(2,1), the size of the intersection of node label sets on any maximal clique in GG is at most 1.

Proof.

Let HH be a maximal clique in G=Jn​(2,1)G=J_{n}(2,1) and S=∩v∈Hν(v).S=\cap_{v\in H}\nu(v). Since every node label set has 2 elements, and any two nodes intersect in exactly one element, it follows that |S|≤1|S|\leq 1. ∎

Both 0 and 1 are possible sizes for the intersection set SS of a maximal clique in G=Jn​(2,1)G=J_{n}(2,1). Moreover, maximal cliques in Jn​(2,1)J_{n}(2,1) are only of two possible sizes according to the size of their intersection set HH. This is shown in Lemma 2.2 below.

Lemma 2.2.

For any maximal clique HH of G=Jn​(2,1)G=J_{n}(2,1), with intersection set SS, for n≥3n\geq 3

|H|={3⇔|S|=0(n−1)⇔|S|=1|{H}|=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccl}3&\iff&|{S}|=0\\ &&\\ (n-1)&\iff&|{S}|=1\end{array}\right.
Proof.

Begin with the smallest non-trivial clique H⊂G=Jn​(2,1)H\subset G=J_{n}(2,1) of size two with vertex label sets ν⁡(v1)={a,b}\nu(v_{1})=\{a,b\} and ν⁡(v2)={b,c}\nu(v_{2})=\{b,c\}, for distinct numbers a,b,c∈[n]a,b,c\in[n]. HH is not maximal for it can be extended by a single node v3v_{3} in one of only two possible ways, as shown below

for a fourth distinct number d∈[n]d\in[n].

Consider first the leftmost triangle. Its intersection set S={a,b}∩{b,c}∩{a,c}=∅S=\{a,b\}\cap\{b,c\}\cap\{a,c\}=\varnothing and |S|=0|{S}|=0. No fourth node, v4v_{4}, can be added and the clique maintained, so this triangle is also a maximal clique. To see this, recall that any node vv adjacent to both v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} must have label set of either {a,c}\{a,c\} or {b,d}\{b,d\}, as shown above. But the first is already in the triangle and the second has no intersection with {a,c}=ν⁡(v3)\{a,c\}=\nu(v_{3}), meaning v4v_{4} cannot be adjacent to v3v_{3}. So, this triangle, with |S|=0|{S}|=0, cannot be extended into a larger clique and, hence, must be maximal of size 3.

Now consider the rightmost triangle. This clique has intersection S={b}S=\{b\} giving |S|=1|{S}|=1, but the clique is maximal only when n=3n=3. For n>4n>4, any node vv with label ν⁡(v)={b,e}\nu(v)=\{b,e\}, where e∈[n]e\in[n] is distinct from aa, bb, cc, and dd, will be adjacent to all nodes in the triangle. There are exactly (n−4)(n-4) such choices remaining in [n][n] to be paired with bb in a label set. The clique can therefore grow maximally to size (n−4)+3=(n−1)(n-4)+3=(n-1) with intersection set S={b}S=\{b\} of size |S|=1|{S}|=1. ∎

Together, Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2 yield the clique number, the size of the maximum clique in G=Jn​(2,1)G=J_{n}(2,1), denoted ω​(Jn​(2,1))\omega(J_{n}(2,1)), as follows:

Corollary 2.3.

The clique number of G=Jn​(2,1)G=J_{n}(2,1), for n≥3n\geq 3, is

ω⁡(Jn​(2,1))=m​a​x​{n−1,3}.\omega(J_{n}(2,1))=max\{n-1,3\}.

According to Lemma 2.2, there are two different types of maximal cliques in Jn​(2,1)J_{n}(2,1). One set, say ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min}, contains maximal cliques H⊂Jn​(2,1)H\subset J_{n}(2,1) having minimal intersection set of size |S|=0|{S}|=0 (with each |H|=3|{H}|=3 for H∈ℳm​i​nH\in\mathcal{M}_{min}); the other, say ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}, contains those maximal cliques having maximal intersection set of size |S|=1|{S}|=1 (with each |H|=n−1|{H}|=n-1 when n≥4n\geq 4 for every H∈ℳm​a​xH\in\mathcal{M}_{max}). The number of maximal cliques of each type is |ℳm​i​n|=(n3)|{\mathcal{M}_{min}}|=\binom{n}{3} and |ℳm​a​x|=(n1)|{\mathcal{M}_{max}}|=\binom{n}{1}.

Figure 1(b) suggests that similar results could exist for the Johnson graph Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) more generally. There, two different types of maximal cliques are shown for G=J5​(3,2)G=J_{5}(3,2). One, shown with dotted line edges, is a 44-clique with intersection set S={1,2,3}∩{1,2,5}∩{1,3,5}∩{2,3,5}=∅S=\{1,2,3\}\cap\{1,2,5\}\cap\{1,3,5\}\cap\{2,3,5\}=\varnothing of size |S|=0|{S}|=0 is in keeping with Lemma 2.2 identifying a maximal clique seemingly in ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} for a J5​(3,2)J_{5}(3,2). Another, shown by thick solid line edges, is of size three and has intersection set S={1,3,4}∩{2,3,4}∩{3,4,5}={3,4}S=\{1,3,4\}\cap\{2,3,4\}\cap\{3,4,5\}=\{3,4\} of size |S|=2|{S}|=2 which is like ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max} in that its intersection set also appears to be of maximum size, though this time 2 instead of 1. More generally, it turns out that maximal cliques in any Johnson graph G=Jn​(m,m−1)G=J_{n}(m,m-1) either have an intersection set of size |S|=0|{S}|=0 or |S|=m−1|{S}|=m-1. This is proved as Theorem 3.4 in the next section.

3 General results

As with Lemma 2.1, the size of an intersection set for any maximal clique of a Johnson graph G=Jn​(m,m−1)G=J_{n}(m,m-1) cannot be larger than m−1m-1, given that is the size of the intersection of node label sets for a single edge. The main result of this section, analogous to Lemma 2.2, proves that this maximum size, m−1m-1, and the minimum size, 0, are the only values possible for the size of the intersection set of a maximal clique in Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1).

In Lemma 2.2, the types of maximal cliques for the simplest case of Jn​(2,1)J_{n}(2,1) were found by beginning with a clique of size two and seeing how it might be expanded by adding nodes. There were only two possible ways to do this, each leading to a different type of maximal clique. Here, we follow the same reasoning, but for vertices and edges from a Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) graph. The figure and proof of Lemma 2.2 guide the intuition in this more general case.

We begin with the case corresponding to the left most diagram of Lemma 2.2. There, a third node, v3v_{3}, was added by selecting the elements for its label set, ν⁡(v3)={a,c}\nu(v_{3})=\{a,c\} from the union of the label sets of the first two vertices v1v_{1} and v2v_{2}, that is ν⁡(v3)⊂B=ν⁡(v1)∪ν⁡(v2)\nu(v_{3})\subset B=\nu(v_{1})\cup\nu(v_{2}). This choice had repercussions in Lemma 2.2 in that the intersection set was null for Jn​(2,1)J_{n}(2,1) and the clique could not be enlarged past size 3 as in the dotted clique of Figure 1 (a). For the dotted clique of Figure 1 (b), however, the set BB for two vertices from a Jn​(3,2)J_{n}(3,2) is larger so that the clique can be enlarged to include a fourth node. In both dotted clique examples of Figure 1 the intersection of the label sets is null.

The next proposition characterizes the intersection sets for maximal cliques, HH, formed in this way from a Johnson graph G=Jn(m.m−1)G=J_{n}(m.m-1).

Proposition 3.1.

Let G=Jn​(m,m−1)G=J_{n}(m,m-1) be a Johnson graph with n≥m+1n\geq m+1 and let HH be a maximal clique in GG. If BB denotes the union

B:=⋃v∈Hν⁡(v),B:=\bigcup_{v\in H}\nu(v),

then ⋂v∈V⁡(H)ν⁡(v)=∅\bigcap_{v\in V(H)}\nu(v)=\varnothing if, and only if, ν⁡(v1)∪ν⁡(v2)=B\nu(v_{1})\cup\nu(v_{2})=B for any v1,v2v_{1},v_{2} distinct in V⁡(H)V(H).

Proof.

Suppose that for any distinct v1,v2∈V⁡(H)v_{1},v_{2}\in V(H), ν⁡(v1)∪ν⁡(v2)=B\nu(v_{1})\cup\nu(v_{2})=B. It follows that for any node v∈V⁡(H),v\in V(H), ν⁡(v)\nu(v) is an m−m-subset of the (m+1)−(m+1)-set BB. Moreover, since every m−m-subset of BB corresponds to a node adjacent to every node in HH, it follows that

ν(V(H))={A:A⊂B,|A|=m}.\nu(V(H))=\{A:A\subset B,|A|=m\}.

For any i∈Bi\in B, the node with label {j∈B:j≠i}\{j\in B:j\neq i\} eliminates ii from the intersection ⋂v∈V⁡(H)ν⁡(v)\bigcap_{v\in V(H)}\nu(v). Thus, the intersection ⋂v∈V⁡(H)ν⁡(v)\bigcap_{v\in V(H)}\nu(v) must be empty.

Conversely, suppose that ⋂v∈V⁡(H)ν⁡(v)=∅\bigcap_{v\in V(H)}\nu(v)=\varnothing. If ν⁡(v1)∪ν⁡(v2)≠B\nu(v_{1})\cup\nu(v_{2})\neq B for some v1,v2∈V⁡(H)v_{1},v_{2}\in V(H), then there exists some v3∈V⁡(H)v_{3}\in V(H) such that x3∈ν⁡(v3)x_{3}\in\nu(v_{3}) and x3∉ν⁡(v1)∪ν⁡(v2)x_{3}\not\in\nu(v_{1})\cup\nu(v_{2}). It follows that v3v_{3} satisfies

ν⁡(v3)=(ν⁡(v1)∩ν⁡(v2))∪{x3}.\nu(v_{3})=\left(\nu(v_{1})\cap\nu(v_{2})\right)\cup\{x_{3}\}.

Thus, v1,v2v_{1},v_{2} and v3v_{3} satisfy the hypothesis of Proposition 3.2 and it follows that ∩v∈V⁡(H)ν(v)\cap_{v\in V(H)}\nu(v) is a set of size m−1m-1, a contradiction.

∎

It would appear, then, that, if we build up a maximal clique in this way, we end with one whose intersection set S=∅S=\varnothing is of size zero. This being the smallest possible intersection set, ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} could again denote the set of such maximal cliques in Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1).

Returning to the intuition followed in the figure of Lemma 2.2, consider how vertices were added when taking the righthand choice. The label set of any third vertex would be formed from the intersection ν⁡(v1)∩ν⁡(v2)\nu(v_{1})\cap\nu(v_{2}), necessarily of size m−1m-1 in Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1), joined by any element of [n][n] not already appearing in the union ν⁡(v1)∪ν⁡(v2)\nu(v_{1})\cup\nu(v_{2}). Following the same logic, vertices could be added providing the intersection set remained of size m−1m-1 until all remaining elements of [n][n] were exhausted, that is, until ν⁡(v1)∪ν⁡(v2)∪⋯∪ν⁡(vr)=[n]\nu(v_{1})\cup\nu(v_{2})\cup\cdots\cup\nu(v_{r})=[n]. For a Johnson Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1), the number of vertices for such a clique would be r=n−(m−1)r=n-(m-1) (e.g., the thick solid line maximal cliques shown in Figures 1). Cliques formed in this fashion, would have largest possible intersection set of size m−1m-1 and so could, again, be denoted ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}.

The next proposition shows that building a maximal clique HH of a Johnson graph G=Jn(m.m−1)G=J_{n}(m.m-1) in this way can only lead to one having largest intersection set of size m−1m-1 and, hence, to H∈ℳm​a​xH\in\mathcal{M}_{max}.

Proposition 3.2.

Let HH be a maximal clique in G=Jn​(m,m−1)G=J_{n}(m,m-1). If |ν⁡(v1)∩ν⁡(v2)∩ν⁡(v3)|=m−1|\nu(v_{1})\cap\nu(v_{2})\cap\nu(v_{3})|=m-1 for some distinct nodes v1,v2,v3∈V⁡(H)v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\in V(H), then

⋂v∈V⁡(H)ν⁡(v)=ν⁡(v1)∩ν⁡(v2).\bigcap_{v\in V(H)}\nu(v)=\nu(v_{1})\cap\nu(v_{2}).
Proof.

Suppose that I:=ν⁡(v1)∩ν⁡(v2)∩ν⁡(v3)I:=\nu(v_{1})\cap\nu(v_{2})\cap\nu(v_{3}) for some distinct nodes v1,v2v_{1},v_{2} and v3v_{3} in HH, and write ν⁡(vj)\nu(v_{j}) in the form {xj}∪I\{x_{j}\}\cup I for j=1,2,3j=1,2,3. If ⋂v∈V⁡(H)ν⁡(v)≠I\bigcap_{v\in V(H)}\nu(v)\neq I, then there must be some i∈Ii\in I for which i∉ν⁡(ui)i\not\in\nu(u_{i}) for some ui∈V⁡(H)u_{i}\in V(H).

Then since ui∈V⁡(H)u_{i}\in V(H) and HH is a clique, ui∼v1,v2,v3u_{i}\sim v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}. Therefore, ν⁡(ui)\nu(u_{i}) must contain xjx_{j} and an (m−2)−(m-2)-subset IjI_{j} from II, for j=1,2,3j=1,2,3. In other words,

ν⁡(ui)=I1∪I2∪I3∪{x1,x2,x3}.\nu(u_{i})=I_{1}\cup I_{2}\cup I_{3}\cup\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\}.

Since II is disjoint from {x1,x2,x3}\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\}, so are the I1,I2,I3I_{1},I_{2},I_{3}. Since the nodes v1,v2,v3v_{1},v_{2},v_{3} are distinct, the variables x1,x2,x3x_{1},x_{2},x_{3} are distinct. Consequently,

|ν⁡(ui)|=|I1∪I2∪I3|+3≥m−2+3=m+1,|\nu(u_{i})|=|I_{1}\cup I_{2}\cup I_{3}|+3\geq m-2+3=m+1,

and such a node cannot exist in Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1). ∎

Should a maximal clique H∈Jn​(m,m−1)H\in J_{n}(m,m-1) belong to one of the two classes ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} and ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}, Propositions 3.1 and 3.2 provide information about HH which is summarized in the following remark.

Remark 3.3.

Maximal cliques H∈Jn​(m,m−1)H\in J_{n}(m,m-1) have the following characteristics unique to which class, ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} or ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}, they belong.

  • •

    H∈ℳm​i​nH\in\mathcal{M}_{min}:

    • –

      The intersection set S=∩v∈V⁡(H)ν(v)=∅S=\cap_{v\in V(H)}\nu(v)=\varnothing with |S|=0|{S}|=0.

    • –

      Node labels of all vertices vj∈V⁡(H)v_{j}\in V(H) are distinct and of the form ν⁡(vj)=B∖{xj}\nu(v_{j})=B\setminus\{x_{j}\} for some B⊂[n]B\subset[n] of size |B|=m+1|{B}|=m+1 and all xj∈Bx_{j}\in B.

    • –

      The size of the maximal clique HH is |H|=|B|=m+1|{H}|=|{B}|=m+1.

    • –

      For any distinct viv_{i}, vjv_{j} in V⁡(H)V(H), ν⁡(vi)∪ν⁡(vj)=B\nu(v_{i})\cup\nu(v_{j})=B.

    • –

      The number of distinct maximal cliques in ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} is (n|B|)=(nm+1)\binom{n}{|{B}|}=\binom{n}{m+1}.

  • •

    H∈ℳm​a​xH\in\mathcal{M}_{max}:

    • –

      The intersection set S=∩v∈V⁡(H)ν(v)S=\cap_{v\in V(H)}\nu(v) has size |S|=m−1|{S}|=m-1.

    • –

      Node labels of all vertices vj∈V⁡(H)v_{j}\in V(H) are distinct and of the form ν⁡(vj)=A∪{xj}\nu(v_{j})=A\cup\{x_{j}\} for some A⊂[n]A\subset[n] of size |A|=m−1|{A}|=m-1 and all xj∈[n]∖Ax_{j}\in[n]\setminus A.

    • –

      The size of the maximal clique HH is |H|=|[n]|−|A|=n−m+1|{H}|=|{[n]}|-|{A}|=n-m+1.

    • –

      For any distinct viv_{i}, vjv_{j} in V⁡(H)V(H), ν⁡(vi)∩ν⁡(vj)=A=S\nu(v_{i})\cap\nu(v_{j})=A=S.

    • –

      The number of distinct maximal cliques in ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max} is (n|A|)=(nm−1)\binom{n}{|{A}|}=\binom{n}{m-1}.

Following the logic of Lemma 2.2, Propositions 3.1 and 3.2 demonstrate at least two distinct classes of maximal cliques exist in Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1), ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} and ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}. That these are the only types of maximal cliques in a Johnson graph G=Jn​(m,m−1)G=J_{n}(m,m-1) is proved in Theorem 3.4 (by induction on mm, with Lemma 2.2 providing the initial case).

Theorem 3.4.

Let HH be a maximal clique in the Johnson graph G=Jn​(m,m−1)G=J_{n}(m,m-1) for n>m≥2n>m\geq 2 and let S=∩v∈Hν(v)S=\cap_{v\in H}\nu(v) be the intersection set of the node labels of HH. Then, |S|∈{0,(m−1)}|{S}|\in\{0,(m-1)\}.

Proof.

The proof proceeds by induction on mm.

Suppose, that there exists m0≥2m_{0}\geq 2 such that, for all n0>m0n_{0}>m_{0}, any maximal clique H0H_{0} in Jn0​(m0,m0−1)J_{n_{0}}(m_{0},m_{0}-1) with intersection set S0=∩v∈H0ν(v)S_{0}=\cap_{v\in H_{0}}\nu(v) has |S0|∈{0,m0−1}|{S_{0}}|\in\{0,m_{0}-1\}. For a proof by induction, we need to show that this implies that for m1=m0+1m_{1}=m_{0}+1, any maximal clique H1H_{1} in Jn1​(m1,m1−1)J_{n_{1}}(m_{1},m_{1}-1), for all n1>m1n_{1}>m_{1}, must have intersection set of size |S1|∈{0,m1−1}|{S_{1}}|\in\{0,m_{1}-1\}.

The inductive step is proved by contradiction. The size of the intersection set of a maximal clique H1H_{1} in Jn1​(m1,m1−1)J_{n_{1}}(m_{1},m_{1}-1) is at most m1−1m_{1}-1, so we assume the intersection set size |S1|=s|{S_{1}}|=s with 0<s<m1−1=m00<s<m_{1}-1=m_{0}. Without loss of generality, we may take the intersection S1S_{1} to be

S1={(n1−s+1),(n1−s+2),…,n1}.S_{1}=\left\{(n_{1}-s+1),(n_{1}-s+2),\ldots,n_{1}\right\}.

Knowing that the node label sets of H1H_{1} have intersection S1S_{1} of size ss and that H1H_{1} induces a maximal clique in Jn1​(m1,m1−1)J_{n_{1}}(m_{1},m_{1}-1), the label set for any vertex vi∈H1v_{i}\in H_{1} can be expressed as ν⁡(vi)=Ii∪S1\nu(v_{i})=I_{i}\cup S_{1} where Ii⊂[n1]I_{i}\subset[n_{1}] with Ii∩S1=∅I_{i}\cap S_{1}=\varnothing and |Ii∩Ij|=m1−1−s|{I_{i}\cap I_{j}}|=m_{1}-1-s for i≠ji\neq j and vi,vj∈H1v_{i},v_{j}\in H_{1}.

This knowledge allows us to construct vertices vj−∈Jn1−1​(m1−1,m1−2)=Jn0​(m0,m0−1)v^{-}_{j}\in J_{n_{1}-1}(m_{1}-1,m_{1}-2)=J_{n_{0}}(m_{0},m_{0}-1) with n0=n1−1>m1−1=m0n_{0}=n_{1}-1>m_{1}-1=m_{0} by simply removing n1∈S1n_{1}\in S_{1} from the node label sets of all vertices in H1H_{1}. That is, for every vi∈V⁡(H1)v_{i}\in V(H_{1}), define vi−∈V⁡(Jn0​(m0,m0−1))v^{-}_{i}\in V(J_{n_{0}}(m_{0},m_{0}-1)) to have node label set ν⁡(vi−)=ν⁡(vi)∖{n1}\nu(v^{-}_{i})=\nu(v_{i})\setminus\{n_{1}\}.

Now consider the graph, H0H_{0}, induced in Jn0​(m0,m0−1)J_{n_{0}}(m_{0},m_{0}-1) by the vertices vi−v^{-}_{i}, so defined. It is easy to see that H0H_{0} is a clique in Jn0​(m0,m0−1)J_{n_{0}}(m_{0},m_{0}-1) – the label sets of its vertices are ν⁡(vi−)=Ii∪S1∖{n1}\nu(v^{-}_{i})=I_{i}\cup S_{1}\setminus\{n_{1}\} with ν⁡(vi−)∩ν⁡(vj−)=(Ii∩Ij)∪S1∖{n1}\nu(v^{-}_{i})\cap\nu(v^{-}_{j})=(I_{i}\cap I_{j})\cup S_{1}\setminus\{n_{1}\} yielding cardinalities of (m1−s)+(s−1)=m1−1=m0(m_{1}-s)+(s-1)=m_{1}-1=m_{0} and (m1−s−1)+(s−1)=m1−2=m0−1(m_{1}-s-1)+(s-1)=m_{1}-2=m_{0}-1, respectively.

To see that H0H_{0} is also maximal, suppose that it is not. Then, there is some vertex v∈Jn0​(m0,m0−1)v\in J_{n_{0}}(m_{0},m_{0}-1) which is not in H0H_{0} but is adjacent to every vertex vi−∈H0v^{-}_{i}\in H_{0}. This adjacency implies

|ν⁡(v)∩(Ii∪S1∖{n1})|=m0−1|{\nu(v)\cap(I_{i}\cup S_{1}\setminus\{n_{1}\})}|=m_{0}-1

for all vi−∈H0v^{-}_{i}\in H_{0}.

We construct a vertex v+∈Jn1​(m1,m1−1)v^{+}\in J_{n_{1}}(m_{1},m_{1}-1) having label set ν⁡(v+)=ν⁡(v)∪{n1}\nu(v^{+})=\nu(v)\cup\{n_{1}\}. Since vv is adjacent to every vi−∈H0v^{-}_{i}\in H_{0}, its intersection with each is of size m0−1=|ν⁡(v)∩(Ii∪S1∖{n1})|m_{0}-1=|{\nu(v)\cap(I_{i}\cup S_{1}\setminus\{n_{1}\})}|. It follows that for vi∈H1v_{i}\in H_{1},

ν⁡(v+)​⋂ν⁡(vi)=ν⁡(v+)​⋂(Ii∪S1)=ν⁡(v+)​⋂[(Ii∪(S1∖{n1}))​⋃{n1}]=[ν⁡(v+)​⋂(Ii∪(S1∖{n1}))]​⋃[ν⁡(v+)∩{n1}]=[ν⁡(v+)​⋂(Ii∪(S1∖{n1}))]​⋃[{n1}]=[(ν⁡(v)∪{n1})​⋂(Ii∪(S1∖{n1}))]​⋃{n1}=[(ν⁡(v)​⋂(Ii∪(S1∖{n1})))​⋃({n1}​⋂(Ii∪(S1∖{n1})))]​⋃{n1}=[(ν⁡(v)​⋂(Ii∪(S1∖{n1})))​⋃∅]​⋃{n1}=[ν⁡(v)​⋂(Ii∪(S1∖{n1}))]​⋃{n1}.\begin{array}[]{rcl}\nu(v^{+})~\bigcap~\nu(v_{i})&=&\nu(v^{+})~\bigcap~(I_{i}\cup S_{1})\\ &&\\ &=&\nu(v^{+})~\bigcap~[(I_{i}\cup(S_{1}\setminus\{n_{1}\}))~\bigcup~\{n_{1}\}]\\ &&\\ &=&[\nu(v^{+})~\bigcap~(I_{i}\cup(S_{1}\setminus\{n_{1}\}))]~\bigcup~[\nu(v^{+})\cap\{n_{1}\}]\\ &&\\ &=&[\nu(v^{+})~\bigcap~(I_{i}\cup(S_{1}\setminus\{n_{1}\}))]~\bigcup~[\{n_{1}\}]\\ &&\\ &=&[(\nu(v)\cup\{n_{1}\})~\bigcap~(I_{i}\cup(S_{1}\setminus\{n_{1}\}))]~\bigcup~\{n_{1}\}\\ &&\\ &=&\left[(\nu(v)~\bigcap~(I_{i}\cup(S_{1}\setminus\{n_{1}\})))~\bigcup~(\{n_{1}\}~\bigcap~(I_{i}\cup(S_{1}\setminus\{n_{1}\})))\right]~\bigcup~\{n_{1}\}\\ &&\\ &=&\left[(\nu(v)~\bigcap~(I_{i}\cup(S_{1}\setminus\{n_{1}\})))~\bigcup~\varnothing\right]~\bigcup~\{n_{1}\}\\ &&\\ &=&\left[\nu(v)~\bigcap~(I_{i}\cup(S_{1}\setminus\{n_{1}\}))\right]~\bigcup~\{n_{1}\}.\\ \end{array}

Now, in square brackets, the left set of the union does not contain n1n_{1} and is of known cardinality m0−1m_{0}-1. It follows, then, that

|ν⁡(v+)​⋂ν⁡(vi)|=|ν⁡(v)​⋂(Ii∪(S1∖{n1}))|+|{n1}|=(m0−1)+1=m1−1.\left|{\nu(v^{+})~\bigcap~\nu(v_{i})}\right|=\left|{\nu(v)~\bigcap~(I_{i}\cup(S_{1}\setminus\{n_{1}\}))}\right|~+~\left|{\left\{n_{1}\right\}}\right|=(m_{0}-1)+1=m_{1}-1.

Hence, v+v^{+} is adjacent to every vertex vi∈H1v_{i}\in H_{1}, and H1H_{1} can be extended to a larger clique in Jn1​(m1,m1−1)J_{n_{1}}(m_{1},m_{1}-1) – a contradiction since H1H_{1} was assumed to be maximal. It follows, then, that no such node, v∈Jn0​(m0,m0−1)v\in J_{n_{0}}(m_{0},m_{0}-1), exists which extends the clique H0H_{0} and, hence, that H0H_{0} must be maximal.

By construction, the intersection set of H0H_{0} is S0=S1∖{n1}S_{0}=S_{1}\setminus\{n_{1}\} and is of size |S0|=s−1|{S_{0}}|=s-1. And, because H0H_{0} is a maximal clique in Jn0​(m0,m0−1)J_{n_{0}}(m_{0},m_{0}-1), by the inductive hypothesis |S0||{S_{0}}| is either 0 or m0−1m_{0}-1. If the latter, then s=m0s=m_{0} is outside the bounds assumed and we have a contradiction. If the former, then, s=1s=1 and, by Proposition 3.1, H0∈ℳm​i​nH_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{min} so S0=∅S_{0}=\varnothing and |S0|=0|{S_{0}}|=0 – again, a contradiction.

It follows that intersecting sets of a maximal clique H1∈Jn​(m1,m1−1)H_{1}\in J_{n}(m_{1},m_{1}-1) with m1=m0+1m_{1}=m_{0}+1 must have size 0 or m1−1m_{1}-1, if it is the case that intersecting sets of a maximal clique H0∈Jn​(m0,m0−1)H_{0}\in J_{n}(m_{0},m_{0}-1) must be of size 0 or m0−1m_{0}-1. The proof by induction is complete by noting that, by Lemma 2.2, the inductive hypothesis holds for m0=2m_{0}=2.

∎

Theorem 3.4 proved that every maximal clique H∈Jn​(m,m−1)H\in J_{n}(m,m-1) has either the minimal or maximal intersection set possible. That is, either H∈ℳm​i​nH\in\mathcal{M}_{min}, or H∈ℳm​a​xH\in\mathcal{M}_{max}. If the former, then |H|=m+1|{H}|=m+1; if the latter, then |H|=n−m+1|{H}|=n-m+1 (see Remark 3.3). As a consequence, we obtain the clique number of Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) for all n≥m+1n\geq m+1.

Corollary 3.5.

The clique number ω⁡(Jn​(m,m−1))\omega(J_{n}(m,m-1)) of the Johnson graph Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) is given by

max⁡(m+1,n−m+1),\max(m+1,n-m+1),

whenever n≥m+1n\geq m+1.

Rewriting, it follows from Corollary 3.5, that the clique number is

ω⁡(Jn​(m,m−1))={m+1ifm+1≤n≤2​mn−m+1if2​m≤n\omega(J_{n}(m,m-1))=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}m+1&\text{if}&m+1\leq n\leq 2m\\ &&\\ n-m+1&\text{if}&2m\leq n\end{array}\right.

and is undefined otherwise.

4 Extending an rr-clique

Given some clique Cr⊂Jn​(m,m−1)C_{r}\subset J_{n}(m,m-1) of size |Cr|=r|{C_{r}}|=r, what can be said about the maximal cliques H⊂Jn​(m,m−1)H\subset J_{n}(m,m-1) that contain it?

We begin with edges (r=2r=2). As the figure in the proof of Lemma 2.2 suggests, every edge in Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) can appear in one clique from ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} and one from ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}. Proposition 4.1 shows that each edge can appear in only one maximal clique in each of ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} and ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}.

Proposition 4.1.

Each edge of Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) will belong to precisely one maximal clique Hm​i​n∈ℳm​i​nH_{min}\in\mathcal{M}_{min} and to precisely one maximal clique Hm​a​x∈ℳm​a​xH_{max}\in\mathcal{M}_{max}.

Proof.

Select any edge ei​je_{ij} connecting vertices viv_{i} and vjv_{j} and let A=ν⁡(vi)∩ν⁡(vj)A=\nu(v_{i})\cap\nu(v_{j}) denote the intersection of their node label sets and B=ν⁡(vi)∪ν⁡(vj)B=\nu(v_{i})\cup\nu(v_{j}) their union.

Define Hm​a​xH_{max} to be the subgraph of Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) induced by the vertex set

V⁡(Hm​a​x)={v∈V⁡(Jn​(m,m−1)):A⊂ν⁡(v)}V(H_{max})=\left\{v\in V(J_{n}(m,m-1)):A\subset\nu(v)\right\}

and Hm​i​nH_{min} that induced by the vertex set

V⁡(Hm​i​n)={v∈V⁡(Jn​(m,m−1)):ν⁡(v)⊂B}.V(H_{min})=\left\{v\in V(J_{n}(m,m-1)):\nu(v)\subset B\right\}.

Vertices viv_{i} and vjv_{j} belong to both sets, so ei​j∈Hm​a​xe_{ij}\in H_{max} and ei​j∈Hm​i​ne_{ij}\in H_{min}.

By construction, Hm​a​x∈ℳm​a​xH_{max}\in\mathcal{M}_{max} and, by Proposition 3.2, there can be no other maximal clique in ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max} containing both viv_{i} and vjv_{j}.

Similarly, Hm​i​n∈ℳm​i​nH_{min}\in\mathcal{M}_{min} and, by Proposition 3.1, any maximal clique in ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} containing both viv_{i} and vjv_{j} must consist of precisely all of the m−m-subsets surrounding the union of the label sets B=ν⁡(vi)∪ν⁡(vj)B=\nu(v_{i})\cup\nu(v_{j}). Again there is no other such maximal clique in ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min}.

Theorem 3.4 completes the proof by guaranteeing that there are no other possible maximal cliques containing both vertices. ∎

Although every edge, or 22-clique, appears in one maximal clique from each of ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} and ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}, this is not the case for any other clique of size r>2r>2. Proposition 4.2 shows that any rr-clique, for r>2r>2, can only appear in one maximal clique, which can only be from one of ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} or ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}.

Proposition 4.2.

Let Cr⊂Jn​(m,m−1)C_{r}\subset J_{n}(m,m-1) be a clique of size r≥2r\geq 2 with Cr⊂HC_{r}\subset H and HH a maximal clique in Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1). Then,

  • •

    H∈ℳm​i​nH\in\mathcal{M}_{min} only if |⋃v∈V⁡(Cr)ν⁡(v)|=m+1~~\left|{\bigcup_{v\in V(C_{r})}\nu(v)}\right|=m+1~~ and |⋂v∈V⁡(Cr)ν⁡(v)|=m+1−r~~\left|{\bigcap_{v\in V(C_{r})}\nu(v)}\right|=m+1-r.

  • •

    H∈ℳm​a​xH\in\mathcal{M}_{max} only if |⋃v∈V⁡(Cr)ν⁡(v)|=m−1+r~~\left|{\bigcup_{v\in V(C_{r})}\nu(v)}\right|=m-1+r~~ and |⋂v∈V⁡(Cr)ν⁡(v)|=m−1~~\left|{\bigcap_{v\in V(C_{r})}\nu(v)}\right|=m-1.

Proof.

Note that every rr-clique, CrC_{r}, in a graph GG is extendible to a maximal clique H⊆GH\subseteq G. When G=Jn​(m,m−1)G=J_{n}(m,m-1), Theorem 3.4 shows that either, H∈ℳm​i​nH\in\mathcal{M}_{min}, or, H∈ℳm​a​xH\in\mathcal{M}_{max} – there are no other possibilities.

Each has implications for the labels on the nodes in CrC_{r}. Without loss of generality, take V⁡(Cr)={v1,…,vr}V(C_{r})=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{r}\} as the vertices of CrC_{r}.

First, consider the case that H∈ℳm​i​nH\in\mathcal{M}_{min}. In Remark 3.3, we note that every node vj∈V⁡(H)v_{j}\in V(H) has node label of the form ν⁡(vj)=B∖{xj}\nu(v_{j})=B\setminus\{x_{j}\} for some set B⊂[n]B\subset[n], xj∈Bx_{j}\in B, and |B|=m+1|{B}|=m+1. Further, B=ν⁡(vi)∪ν⁡(vj)B=\nu(v_{i})\cup\nu(v_{j}) for every pair of distinct nodes vi,vj∈V⁡(H)v_{i},v_{j}\in V(H). In particular, if CrC_{r} extends to H∈ℳm​i​nH\in\mathcal{M}_{min}, then

|⋃v∈V⁡(Cr)ν⁡(v)|=|B|=m+1\left|{\bigcup_{v\in V(C_{r})}\nu(v)}\right|=\left|{B}\right|=m+1

and, for some x1,…,xr∈Bx_{1},\ldots,x_{r}\in B (xjx_{j} peculiar to the node label set of each vj∈V⁡(Cr)v_{j}\in V(C_{r})),

|⋂v∈V⁡(Cr)ν⁡(v)|=|⋂j=1r(B∖{xj})|=|B∖(⋃j=1r{xj})|=m+1−r,\left|{\bigcap_{v\in V(C_{r})}\nu(v)}\right|=\left|{\bigcap_{j=1}^{r}(B\setminus\{x_{j}\})}\right|=\left|{B\setminus(\bigcup_{j=1}^{r}\{x_{j}\})}\right|=m+1-r,

characterize the union and intersection sizes of the label sets for nodes in V⁡(Cr)V(C_{r}) when it is extendible to a maximal clique H∈ℳm​i​nH\in\mathcal{M}_{min}.

Similarly, from Remark 3.3, if CrC_{r} extends to H∈ℳm​a​xH\in\mathcal{M}_{max}, then

|⋃v∈V⁡(Cr)ν⁡(v)|=|⋃j=1r(A∪{xj})|=|A∪(⋃j=1r{xj})|=m−1+r\left|{\bigcup_{v\in V(C_{r})}\nu(v)}\right|=\left|{\bigcup_{j=1}^{r}\left(A\cup\{x_{j}\}\right)}\right|=\left|{A\cup\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^{r}\{x_{j}\}\right)}\right|=m-1+r

for some set A⊂[n]A\subset[n], xj∈[n]∖Ax_{j}\in[n]\setminus A (xjx_{j} peculiar to the node label set of each vj∈V⁡(Cr)v_{j}\in V(C_{r})), and

|⋂v∈V⁡(Cr)ν⁡(v)|=|A|=m−1.\left|{\bigcap_{v\in V(C_{r})}\nu(v)}\right|=\left|{A}\right|=m-1.

∎

When r=2r=2, CrC_{r} is an edge and, by Proposition 4.1, there is both a maximal clique in ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} and one in ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max} which extend CrC_{r}. This is corroborated by the matching set union sizes (m+1m+1) and set intersection sizes (m−1m-1) in Proposition 4.2 when r=2r=2. However, when r>2r>2 these sizes cannot match, and proving that for r>2r>2 any rr-clique CrC_{r} extends to a unique maximal clique in Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) which must be a member of one of ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} or ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}.

Corollary 4.3.

Let Cr⊂Jn​(m,m−1)C_{r}\subset J_{n}(m,m-1) be a clique of size r>2r>2, then CrC_{r} can be extended to only one maximal clique H⊂Jn​(m,m−1)H\subset J_{n}(m,m-1).

Proof.

By Proposition 4.2, CrC_{r} satisfies either |⋃v∈V⁡(Cr)ν⁡(v)|=m+1\left|{\bigcup_{v\in V(C_{r})}\nu(v)}\right|=m+1 or |⋂v∈V⁡(Cr)ν⁡(v)|=m−1\left|{\bigcap_{v\in V(C_{r})}\nu(v)}\right|=m-1, but not both. Thus, there is at least one maximal clique HH which extends CrC_{r}.

If HH is in ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}, then by Proposition 3.2, the intersection of HH must be the intersection of CrC_{r}. Similarly, if HH is in ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min}, then by Proposition 3.1, the union of HH must be the union of CrC_{r}.

In either case, the intersection and union of labels determine the maximal clique HH uniquely. ∎

Corollary 4.3 shows that any clique CrC_{r} of size r>2r>2 can be extended to a maximal clique belonging to only one of ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} or ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}. Proposition 4.2 provides the means for telling which one by examining the size of the intersection or of the union of the node labels of CrC_{r}.

4.1 The clique partition number

Should interest lie in the minimum number of cliques needed to partition the edges of Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1), that is, its clique partition number c​p​(Jn​(m,m−1)CLOSEcp(J_{n}(m,m-1) Erdös et al. ((1988)), then the maximal cliques produced by the edges in Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) provide the solution.

Proposition 4.1 showed that each edge in Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) led to a unique maximum clique in each of ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} and ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}. That each edge will appear in only one element of each set and that the elements are maximal cliques, means that the cliques in either set partition the edges and that they are the fewest possible of that type. It remains only to determine which set, ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} or ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}, is smaller – its size will be the clique partition number. Proposition 4.1 thus yields the following corollary.

Corollary 4.4.

The clique partition number of Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) is given by

c​p​(Jn​(m,m−1))=min⁡{|ℳm​i​n|,|ℳm​a​x|}.cp(J_{n}(m,m-1))=\min\{|{\mathcal{M}_{min}}|,|{\mathcal{M}_{max}}|\}.

Or, to be precise, referring to the sizes of these sets in Remark 3.3, with minimal rewriting, exact expressions may be had as follows.

Corollary 4.5.

The clique partition number of Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) is given by

c​p​(Jn​(m,m−1))={(nm−1)n<2​m(nm+1)n≥2​mcp(J_{n}(m,m-1))=\begin{cases}\dbinom{n}{m-1}&n<2m\\ &\\ \dbinom{n}{m+1}&n\geq 2m\end{cases}

5 Discussion

While the results obtained above apply directly to the cliques and maximal cliques of a Johnson graph, Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1), they may also be expressed in terms of families of intersecting subsets of [n][n] – an intersecting family, ℱ{\cal F}, is a subset of the power set, 𝒫⁡(n)\mathcal{P}({n}), whose elements are pairwise non-disjoint, that is, A∩B≠∅A\cap B\neq\varnothing for every A,B∈ℱA,B\in{\cal F} (Erdős & Kleitman, (1974), e.g., see).

Numerous results have been found for intersection families (Gerbner & Patkós, (2018), e.g., see), including the celebrated Erdős-Ko-Rado (EKR) theorem Erdős et al. ((1961)) which showed that any intersecting family having elements of size k≤m≤12​nk\leq m\leq\frac{1}{2}n, and having no element contained in another (i.e., is an antichain, or Sperner family), had size at most (n−1m−1)\binom{n-1}{m-1}. The EKR bound is obtained by the trivially intersecting family ℱ⊂([n]m){\cal F}\subset\binom{[n]}{m} defined by ℱ={A∈([n]m):x∈A∈[n]}{\cal F}=\{A\in\binom{[n]}{m}~:~x\in A\in[n]\} for some choice of xx. Similarly, Hilton & Milner ((1967)) showed that when ℱ⊂([n]m){\cal F}\subset\binom{[n]}{m} is further restricted to have non-null intersection, ∩A∈ℱA≠∅\cap_{A\in{\cal F}}A\neq\varnothing, across all sets in ℱ{\cal F}, for 2≤m≤12​n2\leq m\leq\frac{1}{2}n, there exists another class of maximal intersecting families within ([n]m)\binom{[n]}{m} whose size is bounded above by (n−1m−1)−(n−m−1m−1)+1\binom{n-1}{m-1}-\binom{n-m-1}{m-1}+1.

The results of the present paper are restricted to intersecting families ℱn,m,m−1⊂([n]m){\cal F}_{n,m,m-1}\subset\binom{[n]}{m} having |A∩B|=m−1|{A\cap B}|=m-1 for distinct A,B∈ℱn,m,m−1A,B\in{\cal F}_{n,m,m-1}. The set of node label sets of the vertices from any maximal clique in Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1) corresponds to a maximally intersecting family ℱ⊂ℱn,m,m−1{\cal F}\subset{\cal F}_{n,m,m-1}.

Theorem 3.4 shows that there are only two possible types of such maximal intersecting families, say ℱm​i​n{\cal F}_{min}, ℱm​a​x⊂ℱn,m,m−1{\cal F}_{max}\subset{\cal F}_{n,m,m-1}, corresponding to the two types of maximal cliques, ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min}, ℳm​a​x⊂Jn​(m,m−1)\mathcal{M}_{max}\subset J_{n}(m,m-1). Expressing Remark 3.3 in terms of intersecting families, there are exactly (nm+1)\binom{n}{m+1} distinct families ℱ∈ℱm​i​n{\cal F}\in{\cal F}_{min} and the following hold for each family ℱ{\cal F}:

  • •

    |∩A∈ℱA|=0|{\cap_{A\in{\cal F}}A}|=0,

  • •

    ∃B⊂[n]\exists B\subset[n] of size m+1m+1 with every A∈ℱA\in{\cal F} having the form B∖{x}B\setminus\{x\} for all x∈Bx\in B,

  • •

    Ai∪Aj=BA_{i}\cup A_{j}=B for all Ai,Aj∈ℱA_{i},A_{j}\in{\cal F}, i≠ji\neq j, and

  • •

    there are m+1m+1 elements in ℱ{\cal F},

and there are (nm−1)\binom{n}{m-1} distinct families ℱ∈ℱm​a​x{\cal F}\in{\cal F}_{max} for each of which the following hold:

  • •

    |∩A∈ℱA|=m−1|{\cap_{A\in{\cal F}}A}|=m-1,

  • •

    ∃B⊂[n]\exists B\subset[n] of size m−1m-1 with every A∈ℱA\in{\cal F} having the form B∪{x}B\cup\{x\} for all x∈[n]∖Bx\in[n]\setminus B,

  • •

    Ai∩Aj=∩A∈ℱAA_{i}\cap A_{j}=\cap_{A\in{\cal F}}A for all Ai,Aj∈ℱA_{i},A_{j}\in{\cal F}, i≠ji\neq j, and

  • •

    there are n−m+1n-m+1 elements in ℱ{\cal F}.

Corollary 3.5 gives the size of the maximal intersecting ℱ⊂([n]m){\cal F}\subset\binom{[n]}{m} restricted to every pair intersection being of size m−1m-1.

Similarly, Proposition 4.2 gives conditions on the size of the union and intersection of sets in a family ℱr⊂ℱn,m,m−1{\cal F}_{r}\subset{\cal F}_{n,m,m-1} of size r≥2r\geq 2 for ℱr{\cal F}_{r} to be extended to a maximally intersecting family of type ℱm​i​n{\cal F}_{min} or ℱm​a​x{\cal F}_{max} – only one of which is possible for r>2r>2.

We again note that Shuldiner & Oldford ((2022)) showed how intersecting families of sets are related to the partition of a set of cliques defining a clique cover for any graph.

Consider again the problem of visualizing high dimensional statistical data which served as our initial motivation. The Johnson graph Jn​(2,1)J_{n}(2,1) has been used successfully in visual data analysis as shown by Oldford & Waddell ((2011)) and Hofert & Oldford ((2017)).

For a Jn​(2,1)J_{n}(2,1) graph, the maximal cliques are either a triangle representing a 3​d3d-space defined by the three variables in the union of the node labels (ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min})(e.g., see Hurley & Oldford, (2011), Figs. 2a and 3), or, an (n−1)(n-1)-clique representing an nn-dimensional space which privileges one of the nn variables to appear in every 2​d2d node (subspace) and swaps one of the remaining variables for another whenever an edge is followed (ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max}). The latter is natural in statistics, for example, when the privileged variable might be regressed upon the second variable at each node (or vice versa).

More generally, for Jn​(m,m−1)J_{n}(m,m-1), traversing maximal cliques in ℳm​i​n\mathcal{M}_{min} is an exploration of an m+1m+1 dimensional space via swapping one of the variables for another with every movement along an edge. Cliques in ℳm​a​x\mathcal{M}_{max} now privilege m−1m-1 variables (e.g. as regressors) while exploring the effect of changing one variable with another (e.g. as response variables in a regression model) for the remaining n−m+1n-m+1 variables with every movement along an edge.
